summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for SNMP management of Multimedia Terminal Adapters in PacketCable and IPCablecom systems. It was later updated by RFC 9141.

plainLanguage.summary:
A multimedia terminal adapter is the box that lets an ordinary telephone work over a cable network. Operators need to see what such a box is doing, and sometimes to tell it to change what it is doing.

Before this RFC, each standards body had its own list of things to read and set, so a management tool had to know which vendor's list to use. This RFC gives them one list: a set of objects covering the device itself, the servers it needs to talk to, and the security relationships it holds, together with two messages the device sends to announce that it has been set up.

questions: what is the packetcable mta mib
what is a multimedia terminal adapter
what are ipcablecom mta snmp objects
how do you reset an mta with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects an operator uses to inspect and control the phone adapters on a cable network.

tldr.problem: Cable operators who offer voice over IP run a box on the customer's premises that connects an ordinary phone to the network. Those boxes were managed with several incompatible vendor MIB modules, so a network management system could not read them the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one IETF MIB module, pktcIetfMtaMib, holding three groups of objects for the device, for the back office servers, and for the security setup, plus two notifications the device sends during provisioning.
tldr.outcome: Management systems get one agreed set of objects for these adapters. Many of them can change the device's behaviour, so the RFC asks for SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy. RFC 9141 later updated this document.

today: RFC 4682 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 9141, which updates the references to the IETF FTP service used for software download.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The MIB module provides a set of objects required for the management of PacketCable, ETSI and ITU-T IPCablecom compliant MTA devices. It is intended to supersede various MTA MIB modules from which it is partly derived: the PacketCable 1.0 MTA MIB Specification, the ITU-T IPCablecom MTA MIB requirements, and the ETSI MTA MIB. The ETSI MTA MIB requirements also refer to various signal characteristics defined in ETSI EN 300 001, Chapter 3, titled Ringing Signal Characteristics, and EN 300 659-1.

Several normative and informative references are used to help define MTA MIB objects. As a convention, wherever PacketCable and IPCablecom requirements are equivalent, the PacketCable reference is used in the object REFERENCE clause, and IPCablecom-compliant MTA devices MUST use the equivalent IPCablecom references.

The module is written to be compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. Managed objects are accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol, and the terms MIB module and information module are used interchangeably, both referring to any of the three types of information modules defined in Section 3 of RFC 2578.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC replaces several rival lists of managed objects with one. Where the two cable standards say the same thing, the list cites one of them and tells equipment built to the other to use its own equivalent.

sections.title: The Devices and the Words
sections.content:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Some of the terms used in the memo are also defined in the PacketCable MTA Device Provisioning Specification and the PacketCable Security Specification.

DOCSIS is the CableLabs Cable Modem project, also known as Data over Cable Service Interface Specification, which defines interface requirements for cable modems involved in high-speed data distribution over cable television system networks; it also refers to the ITU-T J.112 recommendation, Annex B. A Cable Modem acts as a data transport agent used to transfer call management and voice data packets over a DOCSIS-compliant cable system.

A Multimedia Terminal Adapter is a PacketCable- or IPCablecom-compliant device providing telephony services over a cable or hybrid system used to deliver video signals to a community. It contains an interface to endpoints, a network interface, CODECs, and all signaling and encapsulation functions required for Voice over IP transport, call signaling and Quality of Service signaling. An MTA can be embedded or standalone: an Embedded MTA contains an embedded DOCSIS cable modem, while a Standalone MTA is separated from the DOCSIS cable modem by a non-DOCSIS interface such as Ethernet or USB. An Endpoint is a standard RJ-11 telephony physical port on the MTA used for attaching the telephone device.

A Call Management Server is an element of the PacketCable network infrastructure that controls audio connections between MTAs. The Operations Systems Support system is a set of back office software components used for fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management, providing the operations support in deployed PacketCable systems. The Key Distribution Center is an element of the OSS systems functioning as a Kerberos security server, providing mutual authentication of the various components of the PacketCable system, for example between an MTA and a CMS or between an MTA and the Provisioning Server.

A Security Association is a one-way relationship between a sender and a receiver offering security services on the communication flow. A Public Key Certificate is a binding between an entity's public key and one or more attributes relating to its identity. The remaining terms are the standard ones: the X.509 certificate defined in RFC 3280 and RFC 4630, Voice over IP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol of RFC 2131, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol of RFC 1350 and HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines the terms it needs, because several of them are easy to confuse: the adapter with the cable modem built in, the adapter sitting next to it, and the box that connects the telephone itself.

sections.title: The Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The MIB module is identified as pktcIetfMtaMib and is structured in three object groups. pktcMtaDevBase defines the management information pertinent to the MTA device itself. pktcMtaDevServer defines the management information pertinent to the provisioning back office servers. pktcMtaDevSecurity defines the management information pertinent to the PacketCable and IPCablecom security mechanisms.

The first two object groups contain only scalar information objects describing the corresponding characteristics of the MTA device and the back office servers. The third group contains two tables controlling the logical associations between Kerberos realms and Application Servers, that is the Call Management Server and the Provisioning Server. The rows in the tables can be created automatically, for example by the device according to its current state information, or by the management station, depending on the operational situation, so a table may have a mixture of both kinds of rows.

The module also has a pktcMtaDevErrors branch and a conformance section. The whole module is placed at { mib-2 140 }. The module supports a single Provisioning Server, as noted in a comment in the definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is split three ways: what the box is, which servers it should call, and which security relationships it holds. The first two parts are single settings; the third is two tables, one for each kind of relationship.

sections.title: The Device and Server Objects
sections.content:
The pktcMtaDevBase group holds the management information related to the MTA device itself, and some objects used to control the MTA state.

pktcMtaDevSerialNumber contains the serial number of the MTA, and its value MUST be identical to the value specified in DHCP option 43, sub-option 4. pktcMtaDevEndPntCount contains the number of endpoints present in the managed MTA and has the range 1 to 255. pktcMtaDevProvisioningState describes the completion state of the MTA initialization process. pktcMtaDevEnabled controls the administrative state of the MTA endpoints: set to true the MTA is administratively enabled and MUST be able to interact with the PacketCable entities such as the CMS, the Provisioning Server, the KDC, and other MTAs and MGs on all PacketCable interfaces; set to false the MTA is administratively disabled and MUST shut down all media sessions, shut down Network Control Signaling by following the Restart in Progress procedures in the PacketCable NCS specification, maintain the SNMP interface for management and the SNMP key management interface, and not continue Kerberized key management with CMSes until it is set back to true. The MTA must execute all actions required to enable or disable the telephony services for all endpoints immediately upon receipt of an SNMP SET operation.

pktcMtaDevResetNow is used to instruct the MTA to reset. Reading it always returns false, and setting it to true causes the device to reset immediately, with all connections flushed locally, all current actions such as ringing immediately terminated, requests for signaling notifications flushed, all endpoints disabled, and the provisioning flow started at step MTA-1. If a value is written into an instance of this object, the agent MUST NOT retain the supplied value across MTA re-initializations or reboots. The same applies to the value written into an instance of pktcMtaDevEnabled.

The pktcMtaDevServer group holds the management information describing the back office servers and the parameters related to the communication timers, together with some objects controlling the initial MTA interaction with the Provisioning Server. pktcMtaDevServerDhcp1 and pktcMtaDevServerDhcp2 hold the IP addresses of the primary and secondary DHCP servers designated for MTA provisioning, and pktcMtaDevServerDns1 and pktcMtaDevServerDns2 the primary and secondary DNS servers used by the managed MTA to resolve the Fully Qualified Domain Name and IP addresses. pktcMtaDevConfigFile contains the name of the provisioning configuration file the managed MTA must download from the Provisioning Server. pktcMtaDevProvConfigHash contains the hash value of the MTA configuration file calculated over its content, and when the managed MTA downloads the file it authenticates the configuration file using the hash value provided in this object.

A textual convention, PktcMtaDevProvEncryptAlg, lists the algorithms usable to encrypt the configuration file: none(0) for no encryption, des64CbcMode(1) for a DES 64-bit key in CBC mode, t3Des192CbcMode(2) for a 3DES 192-bit key in CBC mode, aes128CbcMode(3) for an AES 128-bit key in CBC mode and aes256CbcMode(4) for an AES 256-bit key in CBC mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of these objects are readings: the serial number, how many phone sockets the box has, which servers it should use. A few are switches: one turns telephony on and off, one reboots the box. The configuration file the box downloads can be protected with one of five listed encryption algorithms, including none at all.

sections.title: Security Associations and the Two Tables
sections.content:
The pktcMtaDevSecurity group holds the management information describing the security-related characteristics of the managed MTA. It contains two tables describing the logical dependencies and parameters needed to establish Security Associations between the MTA and other Application Servers, that is the back office components and the Call Management Servers.

The realm table, pktcMtaDevRealmTable, is used in conjunction with any Application Server that communicates securely with the managed MTA, whether a CMS or the Provisioning Server, and defines the Kerberos realms for those servers. The CMS table, pktcMtaDevCmsTable, contains the parameters describing the establishment of the Security Association between the MTA and CMSes, and defines the CMS within the domains. Each MTA endpoint is associated with one CMS at any given time. The realm table is indexed by an Index Counter and contains a conceptual column with the Kerberos realm name, and the CMS table is indexed by an Index Counter and contains the CMS Fully Qualified Domain Name, with each row holding the Kerberos realm name associated with that name, so that each CMS can exist in a different Kerberos realm.

The establishment of a Security Association between an MTA and an Application Server is described in the PacketCable Security Specification and consists of two steps. The first is the Authentication Server Exchange, which provides mutual authentication between the parties, that is between an MTA and an Authentication Server; the process is defined by a number of parameters grouped per realm, and these are gathered in the realm table. The second is the Application Server Exchange, which allows the establishment of Security Associations between authenticated parties; the CMS table holds the parameters for that process between an MTA and a CMS.

The module also contains scalar objects in the server group that define various parameters for the Application Server Exchange between an MTA and the Provisioning Server: pktcMtaDevProvUnsolicitedKeyMaxTimeout, pktcMtaDevProvUnsolicitedKeyNomTimeout, pktcMtaDevProvUnsolicitedKeyMaxRetries and pktcMtaDevProvSolicitedKeyTimeout.

On secure software download, E-MTAs are embedded with DOCSIS 1.1 cable modems and have their software upgraded by the cable modem according to the DOCSIS requirements. Although that is the case, S-MTAs implement a specific mechanism for Secure Software Download, which provides a means to verify the code upgrade using Code Verification Certificates and is modelled after the DOCSIS mechanism implemented in cable modems. This is why the MTA MIB and the S-MTA compliance modules also rely on two MIB object groups: docsBpi2CodeDownloadGroup, defined in the IETF BPI Plus MIB module, and docsDevSoftwareGroupV2, defined in the IETF Cable Device v2 MIB module.

E-MTAs must use the authentication mechanism based on X.509 Public Key Infrastructure certificates, and the value of the pktcMtaDevRealmOrgName object should contain the X.509 organization name attribute of the Telephony Service Provider certificate. X.509 attributes are defined using UTF-8 string encoding, where a character can take one to six octets, although the current version of UTF-8 does not require more than four octets to encode a valid code point.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the adapter can talk to the call server, the two authenticate each other and set up a protected flow. That needs two pieces of information: which servers are trusted, and in which Kerberos realm each one sits. The MIB holds both as tables that an operator can fill in.

sections.title: Provisioning States and Notifications
sections.content:
The pktcMtaDevProvisioningState object has the syntax INTEGER with seven values, and it indicates the completion state of the MTA device provisioning process. If the configuration file could be parsed successfully and the MTA is able to reflect the same in its MIB, the MTA MUST return pass. If the MTA is in the process of being provisioned, it MUST return inProgress. If the configuration file was in error due to incorrect values in the mandatory parameters, the MTA MUST reject the configuration file and return failConfigFileError. If the configuration file had proper values for all the mandatory parameters but has errors in any of the optional parameters, including any vendor-specific object identifiers that are incorrect or not known to the MTA, the MTA MUST return passWithWarnings. If the configuration file is valid but the MTA cannot reflect the same in its configuration, for example because too many entries caused memory exhaustion, it must accept the CMS configuration entries related and the MTA MUST return passWithIncompleteParsing. If the configuration file cannot be parsed because of an internal error, the MTA MUST return failureInternalError, and if it cannot accept the configuration file for any other reason it MUST return failureOtherReason. When a final SNMP INFORM is sent as part of Step 25 of the MTA provisioning process, this value is also included in the final INFORM message.

Two notifications are defined. pktcMtaDevProvisioningEnrollment is an INFORM notification issued by the MTA to initiate the PacketCable provisioning process when the MTA SNMP enrollment mechanism is used; it contains the system description, the current software version, the MTA device type identifier, the MTA MAC address obtained in the MTA ifTable in the ifPhysAddress object corresponding to ifIndex 1, and a correlation ID. pktcMtaDevProvisioningStatus is an INFORM notification that may be issued by the MTA to confirm the completion of the PacketCable provisioning process and to report its provisioning completion status; it contains the MTA MAC address, a correlation ID and the MTA provisioning state.
sections.plainLanguage: The box reports how its setup went in one of seven ways, from still in progress to a clean pass to a specific failure. It also sends two messages: one to say it has arrived and needs setting up, and one afterwards to say how it went.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a number of management objects defined in the module with a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. Improper manipulation of the objects defined in this MIB may result in random behavior of MTA devices and may result in service disruption.

The RFC lists the sensitive objects. If set maliciously, pktcMtaDevResetNow and pktcMtaDevEnabled would cause the MTA device to reset or stop its service. All writable objects in the pktcMtaDevServer group and some in the realm table share the potential, if set maliciously, to prevent the MTA from provisioning properly, and are therefore considered very sensitive for service delivery. Two of them have additional specific vulnerabilities: pktcMtaDevServerDns1 and pktcMtaDevServerDns2 could prevent the MTA from being authenticated and consequently from getting telephony services, and pktcMtaDevRealmStatus could cause the whole row of the table to be deleted, which may prevent the MTA from getting telephony services.

All writable objects in the CMS table share the potential, if set maliciously, to disrupt the telephony service by altering which Call Management Server the MTA must send signalling registration to. Some writable objects in the realm table will not have an immediate effect on service but may impact performance and cause avalanche attacks on provisioning and Kerberos KDC servers, especially after massive device reboots: pktcMtaDevResetKrbTickets causes the MTA to request a new Kerberos ticket at reboot, and pktcMtaDevRealmPkinitGracePeriod and pktcMtaDevRealmTgsGracePeriod cause the MTA to renew its tickets more frequently when set to short periods.

Some readable objects may also be considered sensitive. The values of the DHCP server addresses and of pktcMtaDevSnmpEntity may be used to launch denial-of-service attacks against the Telephony Service Provider DHCP or Provisioning servers, and the values of pktcMtaDevProvKerbRealmName, pktcMtaDevManufacturerCertificate, pktcMtaDevCertificate and pktcMtaDevTelephonyRootCertificate may be used to launch denial-of-service attacks against Kerberos servers. One further readable object may expose security threats: pktcMtaDevFQDN may include sensitive information about the domain name, and potentially the domain topology. It is thus important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control as to who on the secure network is allowed to access and read, change, create or delete the objects in this MIB module. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is then a customer or operator responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is properly configured to give access to the objects only to those principals that have legitimate rights to read or change them.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of these settings can break the phone service or stop the box from being set up, so they need protecting. The RFC's advice is to use SNMPv3 with its authentication and encryption, and to decide carefully who is allowed to change what.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content: The MIB module defined in the document uses the IANA-assigned object identifier value { mib-2 140 }, recorded in the SMI Numbers registry, for the module identifier pktcIetfMtaMib.
sections.plainLanguage: The module was given one number in IANA's registry of management objects, so that a management tool can find it by name.

viz.caption: THE OBJECT TREE OF THE MTA MIB (RFC 4682)

items.label: pass
items.desc: The configuration file parsed and the MTA reflects it in its MIB.

items.label: inProgress
items.desc: The MTA is in the process of being provisioned.

items.label: failConfigFileError
items.desc: Mandatory parameters were wrong, so the configuration file was rejected.

items.label: passWithWarnings
items.desc: Mandatory parameters were right but some optional ones were wrong.

items.label: passWithIncompleteParsing
items.desc: The file was valid but the MTA could not store all of it.

items.label: failureInternalError
items.desc: The configuration file could not be parsed because of an internal error.

items.label: failureOtherReason
items.desc: The configuration file was refused for some other reason.

viz.caption: HOW A SECURITY ASSOCIATION IS ESTABLISHED

items.title: Step one: authentication
items.text: The AS-exchange gives mutual authentication between the MTA and an authentication server. Its parameters are grouped per realm and live in the realm table.

items.title: Step two: application exchange
items.text: The AP-exchange sets up the protected flow between the now-authenticated parties. Its parameters for a CMS live in the CMS table.

items.title: The realm table
items.text: Holds the Kerberos realms of the application servers, indexed by a counter, with a column for the realm name.

items.title: The CMS table
items.text: Holds each call server's fully qualified domain name and the realm it belongs to, so different servers can sit in different realms.

viz.caption: THE TWO NOTIFICATIONS SENT DURING PROVISIONING

messages.label: INFORM: pktcMtaDevProvisioningEnrollment
messages.note: Says the device has arrived and asks to be provisioned. Carries the system description, software version, device type, MAC address and a correlation ID.

messages.label: INFORM: pktcMtaDevProvisioningStatus
messages.note: Reports how provisioning went, with the MAC address, the correlation ID and the provisioning state.
